title: Your anthology
hook: collect lines from this block of poets: blend them like Seneca's honey, or name each flower like Meleager?
tomorrow: the cowherd who left the party whenever the harp came near. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: her music. Hildegard's Devil never sings, because for her song is the praise of heaven. Now the poets are nearly done, and it's time to gather what they gave you.

A screenshot folder of lines. A quote taped above a desk. That's an anthology, whether or not anyone calls it one. And two old voices disagree about how to keep it. The Roman Stoic Seneca says: blend them, the way bees blend flowers into honey. A Greek poet named Meleager says: keep every flower, and say whose it is. Before the poets close tomorrow, let both of them make their case.
screen: `A FOLDER OF SCREENSHOTS.` → `SENECA: BLEND LIKE HONEY.` → `MELEAGER: NAME EVERY FLOWER.`

segments.voice: Meleager gathered short poems by many poets into one collection and called it the Garland. In his opening poem he weaves each poet in as a flower, by name: lilies from one poet, and from Sappho only a few blooms, but roses. Nobody gets melted into anyone else. You can still see every flower. Seneca, writing to his friend Lucilius, takes the other side, and his case is strong. Bees, he says, wander from flower to flower and then work what they've gathered into something new. Do the same with your reading: blend it into one flavor, so that even when people can tell where it came from, it's become yours. Food that sits in the stomach whole is a burden; digested, it turns into strength. A line you only copy and never chew stays someone else's. Here's where this path stands, the way it has all through the poets. On names, it takes Meleager's side. Rumi stays a Muslim mystic in Konya, Dickinson a poet in her Amherst room, each line tagged with its own world and never stirred into one new teaching. On digesting, it takes Seneca's. A line you don't carry into an ordinary Tuesday is decoration. So your anthology is a garland on the page, every flower named, and honey in you.
screen: `MELEAGER'S GARLAND: EVERY POET NAMED.` · `SENECA'S BEES: BLEND IT INTO HONEY.` · `ON NAMES, THE GARLAND.` · `ON DIGESTING, THE HONEY.` · then, large: `MY ANTHOLOGY.`

segments.voice: On a fresh page, copy out the lines from these poets that stayed with you, as many as come, up to ten. After each one, write the poet's name. Don't look anything up yet; the ones that come back on their own are already part honey.
Your anthology: the lines you've gathered from the poets, kept like a garland with every name on it, and carried like honey.
For today: my anthology, every flower named and every line digested into you. That's day 1585.

howItsDone: Readers in many traditions keep commonplace books, notebooks of copied lines with their sources; anthologies from Meleager's Garland onward gather poets side by side under their own names.

tie.story: Meleager wove every poet into his Garland by name, while Seneca told Lucilius to blend his reading like honey.

Seneca.meaning: a Roman Stoic philosopher who wrote letters to his friend Lucilius

Meleager.meaning: a Greek poet who gathered many poets into his Garland

Sappho.meaning: an ancient Greek poet from the island of Lesbos

Lucilius.meaning: Seneca's friend, to whom he wrote his letters

Konya.meaning: the city in Anatolia where Rumi lived and taught
